RITIDIAN: A view of the ocean from the Ritidian Overlook in Dededo. David Castro/The Guam Daily Post

President Donald Trump's proclamation this month restoring commercial fishing in Pacific marine national monuments, including the Islands Unit of the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument, has drawn measured but watchful responses from Guam officials and island legislators, who say the move is neither the windfall nor the threat it might appear.

Gov. Lou Leon Guerrero said the question of balancing natural preservation with food security and the right of a people to live off the ocean as their ancestors did is complex, and that no one should represent the views of an entire people without meaningful community discussion and study.

"Yes, our political status may give the federal government the power to make these decisions without consulting us, but having the power to do it that way doesn't mean it should be done," Leon Guerrero told The Guam Daily Post. "The ocean knows no political boundaries and just as preservation efforts can help protect reefs and fish stock far beyond an area outlined on a map, activities such as overfishing or deep-sea mining or others can have impacts beyond those same political boundaries."

The administration said it remains informed and involved through its participation in the Western Pacific Regional Fishery Management Council, known as the Westpac Council, and is still working through the implications of the proclamation, including whether it reverts to prior regulations that may have limited entry permits for specific fisheries.

"Much of the heavy lifting takes place in Washington, where we will continue to speak with a unified voice that includes actively engaging federal officials on the realities in the water and on the ground here in the Pacific," Leon Guerrero said. "It's also important to recognize that there are legal rights and responsibilities at play here. This could mean the legal intervention of non-profit environmental advocates could happen and that has been effective in the past."

Chelsa Muña, director of the Guam Department of Agriculture and Guam's representative on the Westpac Council, said she does not expect the proclamation to produce a rush of outside fishing vessels into Mariana waters, at least not right away.

"I don't really anticipate much of an effect because even prior to the monument being established, no one fished in the waters commercially," Muña told the Post. "Not since maybe around the 70s and 80s."

The waters sit roughly 400 miles from Guam, and the economics of sending large commercial vessels that far out are a significant barrier. Longliners and purse seiners from the U.S. mainland, she said, would face steep costs with limited return.

"If you think about that, that's people from either the west coast, or the east coast of the United States, or the southern Gulf Coast, traveling all the way to the Mariana Islands to fish in our waters," Muña said. "It's just not economically feasible for them."

The proclamation, signed June 11, opens commercial fishing access in portions of the Papahānaumokuākea Marine National Monument near Hawai'i, the Rose Atoll Marine National Monument near American Samoa, and the Islands Unit of the Mariana Trench Marine National Monument, encompassing waters around the Northern Mariana Islands chain.

A key distinction Muña drew is between subsistence and commercial fishing. Under the monument plan in place before the proclamation, local fishers could access the waters for subsistence purposes. No formal commercial fishing regulations for the monument had been established.

With commercial access now permitted in principle, Muña said the path forward for Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands is to establish regulations that reflect local interests through an open public process.

"When we establish the regulations, that'll be an open public process," she said. "So the public will have the opportunity to comment on any draft or final regulations."

Muña said Guam and the CNMI have been working together to develop a legitimate commercial fishery for both islands, coordinating with the Western and Central Pacific Fisheries Commission and the Westpac Council. She pointed to Papahānaumokuākea, where commercial fishing permits are capped at nine at a time, as a model for how the Mariana Trench monument could be managed.

"It's not just a free-for-all," Muña said. "Commercial fishers want the fishery to be sustainable. They don't want to harvest it to the point of diminishing their own resource. Otherwise, they don't have a business."

The proclamation drew sharp criticism from Angelo Villagomez, a CHamoru and senior fellow for conservation policy at the Center for American Progress, who said the rollback feels like a direct attack on cultural heritage and the ecosystems of a resource previously reserved for the CHamoru and Refaluwasch people. In an earlier interview with the Post, Villagomez acknowledged the practical change on the water may not be dramatic, but said waters once reserved exclusively for indigenous fishers are now open to wealthy American fishermen. The monument protections were originally established by Republican President George W. Bush. The Mariana Trench Marine National Monument was designated in 2009.

The board of Friends of the Mariana Trench called the signing a direct erosion of Pacific cultural heritage, saying in a statement the fight for healthy oceans and the communities that depend on them is far from over.

Sen. Jesse Lujan, who chairs the Committee on Transportation, Tourism, Customs, Utilities, and Federal and Foreign Affairs, told the Post Guam must approach the issue with balance.

"Food security and economic opportunity are important, especially for island communities, but so are conservation, fisheries sustainability and protection of ocean resources that are central to our culture and way of life," he said. "This is not just a question of supporting or opposing federal action. It is about making sure Guam has a seat at the table."

Sen. Chris Barnett came out firmly against the proclamation, saying the reasoning behind the monument's establishment remains valid and that rolling back those protections appears politically motivated.

"It's disappointing to see the rollback of protections like these, for what really looks like partisan and political reasons," he told the Post, adding that Guam's congressional representative should push back even if it means going against party leadership.

Sen. William Parkinson said in a written response to the Post that any expanded access must come with clear requirements that local communities benefit directly.

"Food security cannot be used as a slogan while the benefits go to distant commercial fleets," Parkinson said. "If fish are caught near the Marianas but never land in Guam, that does nothing for our people. No blank check for industrial fishing in protected waters."

Sen. Telo Taitague told the Post the issue was only recently brought to her attention and she needs more research before drawing any conclusions, but added, "I am very concerned about any environmental development that could impact our people."

Muña said a group or a steering committee for the Mariana Trench may have been recently stood up by the governor to begin developing monument regulations. The Post was not immediately able to independently confirm any specific appointments.

"It's not just one or the other when it comes to conservation and economy," Muña said. "They have to work together to make it sustainable for both."
